item.title: What You Actually Pulled: Reading Quantisation, Parameter Count and Context Out of an Ollama GGUF File
item.description: A 31B tag pulls 18.99 GiB of layers — an 18,670,033,120-byte model blob against 61.4 GB for the same weights in bf16 — and nothing ollama prints says which quantisation is inside. An 8–32 MiB ranged read of the GGUF header returns the tensor table, so bits per weight, parameter count and the declared context field become numbers you can check before the download finishes.
item.content:encoded:
You pulled a tag. The download is 18.99 GiB for a model the card calls 31B. The agent that needed long history behaves as if it had a fraction of the context the card advertises. The quality does not match the benchmark chart that made you choose the model in the first place. None of those three surprises is a property of the model. All three are properties of the artifact: which quantisation the tag actually resolved to, how many bits per weight that quantisation really costs, and which metadata value declares the context this particular build was made for.

This article answers those three questions from the bytes rather than from the tag name. Every figure below comes from a ranged HTTP read of the file header — 8 to 32 MiB out of a 5–19 GB file — so no weights were downloaded, no server was started, and no throughput, quality or VRAM claim is made or implied. Five artifacts were read on 2026-11-06: three published GGUF files and two Ollama registry blobs.

The file on disk does not match the card

The unsloth repository unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF lists its bf16 build as two shards of 49,950,156,960 and 11,463,033,568 bytes, which is 61,413,190,528 bytes or 57.2 GiB (repository index). The same index lists gemma-4-31B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf at 18,323,733,440 bytes. That is 17.07 GiB, 18.32 decimal GB, and 3.35× smaller than the bf16 build.

So “18 GB, not 48 GB” contains two separate confusions. The 18 figure is real: it is the 4-bit file, and it looks smaller in GiB than in decimal GB because binary units divide by 1,073,741,824. The 48 figure corresponds to nothing in that repository — the bf16 weights there are 61.41 decimal GB, and a Q8_0 build of the same weights lands at 8.5 bits per weight rather than 16. Once the quantisation is known, both sizes are arithmetic.

The catch is that 31B is a name, not a specification. The name tells you the parameter class; it says nothing about the 4.77 bits per weight the file actually spends. ollama show prints a Modelfile back at you, and that Modelfile is a description of how to load the blob, not of what is inside it. The manifest audit in the tag-size article takes the first step: it divides a manifest’s model-layer bytes by the parameter total published by the model repository, and states plainly that it did not inspect tensors. This piece takes the second step and reads the tensor table, so numerator and denominator come from the same file.

GGUF is a directory inside a file

A GGUF file begins with the magic GGUF, a version, a tensor count and a metadata key/value count, then a metadata block of typed key/value pairs, then one tensor-info record per tensor holding its name, dimensions, quantisation type and byte offset. The weight data starts after that array, padded to the alignment boundary, and each tensor offset is relative to the start of the data section rather than to the start of the file (GGUF specification).

That layout is what makes a header read sufficient. The tensor-info array carries the type of every tensor and the size of every dimension, so the full weight map — how many bytes at which precision, how many elements in total — is available before a single weight is fetched. The weights themselves are only needed to run the model, not to describe it.

Reading it without downloading it

The probe sends two requests per artifact. A HEAD gives Content-Length, the exact size of the file. A GET with Range: bytes=0-33554431 returns the first 32 MiB, which is enough for the metadata block, the tokenizer arrays and the tensor-info array of a 262,144-token vocabulary.

The window has to clear the header, and how much that takes is a property of the file, not a constant. A 1 MiB window fails on the Gemma file before the tensor table is complete (EOFError: window ended at 1048576; need 13 more), and 8 MiB still fails there (window ended at 8388608; need 8 more) because the 262,144-token vocabulary pushes the weight section out to byte 15,834,176. The same 8 MiB window was already enough for both Qwen3 files, whose weight sections start at 5,956,416 and 5,956,384 bytes. In the saved batch three artifacts parsed at 32 MiB — the Gemma file and both registry blobs — and two parsed at 8 MiB (Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M at 14:34:01Z, Qwen3-8B-Q8_0 at 14:34:04Z); a later 32 MiB rerun of Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M at 14:41:15Z reproduced the same values. The parser raises on a short window instead of returning the tensors it managed to read, which matters: a silently truncated tensor list still produces a plausible-looking bits-per-weight number that is simply wrong.

The five successful reads ran between 14:34:01Z and 14:34:33Z on 2026-11-06, each returning HTTP 206 and taking 1.41–4.03 s of wall clock. The two registry blobs answered fastest (1.41 s and 1.62 s) and the Gemma file slowest (4.03 s), a spread that tracks the origin rather than the 8- or 32-MiB span. The SHA-256 of each fetched span was recorded so a later rerun can prove it read the same bytes.

Worked example: gemma-4-31B-it Q4_K_M

The file’s header declares architecture gemma4, 60 blocks, 262,144 tokens of context, and 833 tensors. Adding up the dimensions gives 30,697,345,596 stored elements — the parameter count of this file, not of the family. Multiplying each tensor’s element count by its type’s block width gives 18,307,897,584 bytes of weights.

Quantisation Tensors Bytes Share of weight bytes
Q4_K (4.5 bpw nominal) 356 15,006,007,296 81.96%
Q6_K (6.5625 bpw nominal) 55 3,296,563,200 18.01%
F32 (32 bpw) 422 5,327,088 0.03%

8 × 18,307,897,584 ÷ 30,697,345,596 = 4.7712 bits per weight. The 422 F32 tensors are almost all small norms and biases: they are 422 of the 833 tensor records but 0.03% of the bytes.

The reconciliation is what makes that ratio trustworthy rather than decorative. The weight section begins at byte 15,834,176, so the file’s published size leaves 18,307,899,264 bytes for weights. The tensor table accounts for 18,307,897,584 of them — a residue of 1,680 bytes, 0.00001%, which is the alignment padding after the final tensor. A wrong block table, a missed tensor or a misread dimension cannot land on that total by accident.

Why “4-bit” is 4.77 and “8-bit” is 8.50

Block geometry explains the gap between the label and the measurement. In llama.cpp’s quantisation table a K-quant block covers 256 elements: Q4_K spends 144 bytes per block (4.5 bpw), Q6_K spends 210 (6.5625 bpw), and Q8_0 — a 32-element block — spends 34 (8.5 bpw) (constants.py).

A Q4_K_M file is a mixture. The _M variant keeps selected tensors at a higher precision, so on the Gemma file 18.01% of weight bytes are Q6_K and the blended figure is 4.7712 rather than 4.5. The Qwen3-8B Q4_K_M file shows the same mechanism at a different ratio: 3,704,979,456 bytes of Q4_K, 1,315,614,720 of Q6_K and 1,232,896 of F32 over 8,190,735,360 elements, giving 4.9049 bpw with 26.20% of weight bytes at Q6_K. The Q8_0 build of the same 8.19B parameters spends 8,702,328,832 bytes at Q8_0 plus the same 1,232,896 bytes of F32 and measures 8.5009.

The practical consequence: “4-bit” and “8-bit” are labels for a mixture, and the blended figure moves with how much of the file the quantizer kept at higher precision. If the number matters — and it does when you are deciding whether a file fits in VRAM or on a laptop disk — it has to be summed from the tensors.

The tag is not the file

An Ollama tag resolves to a registry manifest, and that manifest names layers with exact byte sizes and digests. Reading the model layer of gemma4:31b and parsing it the same way gives a different file from the same-named Hugging Face build.

Artifact Bytes Q4_K bytes Q6_K bytes Parameters bpw
HF gemma-4-31B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf 18,323,733,440 15,006,007,296 3,296,563,200 30,697,345,596 4.7712
Ollama gemma4:31b model layer 18,670,033,120 14,250,442,752 4,398,428,160 30,697,345,596 4.8614

Same architecture, same 60 blocks, same 262,144-token context field, same parameter count — 346,299,680 more bytes, and a different mixture: 23.58% of the tag’s weight bytes are Q6_K against 18.01% in the Hugging Face file. The manifest’s own from field names the upstream publisher tag dhiltgen/gemma4:31b-it-mtp-q4_K_M-llamacpp, not a Hugging Face repository, so size and mixture similarity cannot establish which repository this blob was converted from. Treat provenance as unknown and check the bytes you have.

The same divergence appears at 8B. The Ollama qwen3:8b model layer is 5,225,374,496 bytes against 5,027,783,488 for Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf, and it carries 301,989,888 bytes of F16 tensors the Hugging Face Q4_K_M does not, with 1,253,683,200 bytes of Q6_K against 1,315,614,720. Bits per weight: 5.0979 versus 4.9049, over an identical 8,190,735,360 parameters.

A tag can also be more than one model. gemma4:31b is projector 1,200,726,368 + model 18,670,033,120 + draft 514,687,072 bytes — 20,385,446,560 weight-bearing bytes, and 20,385,457,992 bytes across every layer including template, license and params. That is 18.99 GiB of download for a file advertised as 31B at 4-bit. The projector is a separate artifact with its own cost profile, covered in the projector article; it is not part of a weights-only bits-per-weight ratio, and adding it to the denominator would make the number meaningless.

Which context value wins

Three different quantities get called “the context length”, and they are not interchangeable.

The first is the field inside the artifact. Parsing the metadata block gives gemma4.context_length = 262144 and qwen3.context_length = 40960. For the Qwen3-8B files that 40,960 is the positional-embedding allocation the vendor ships in config.json as max_position_embeddings; it is not a statement of the length the weights were trained on.

The second is the model card’s own framing, which states the limits separately: “Context Length: 32,768 natively and 131,072 tokens with YaRN”. The card then explains where 40,960 comes from: “The default max_position_embeddings in config.json is set to 40,960. This allocation includes reserving 32,768 tokens for outputs and 8,192 tokens for typical prompts, which is sufficient for most scenarios involving short text processing” (Qwen3-8B card). Read as three numbers rather than one: 32,768 native, 131,072 with YaRN scaling, and 40,960 as a padded default that splits into an 8,192-token prompt budget and 32,768 reserved for generation. An agent carrying a 30k-token tool history is asking for more prompt than that arrangement allows, on a card whose headline number reads “40,960”.

The third is the runtime option, and it is the one that decides what is actually served. Ollama’s Modelfile reference defines PARAMETER num_ctx 4096 as setting “the context window size to 4096, this controls how many tokens the LLM can use as context to generate the next token” (Modelfile reference), and a tag’s params layer is where such a value would be baked in. Both tags’ params layers are readable: the registry blob URL answers HTTP 307 to a presigned object URL, and following it returns 64 bytes for gemma4:31b (draft_num_predict, temperature, top_k, top_p) and 120 bytes for qwen3:8b (repeat_penalty, stop, temperature, top_k, top_p). Neither contains num_ctx, so neither tag pins a window. What is established is the boundary: the artifact’s declared length is not the served length, the tag’s params do not set it, and the value that does comes from a server default or a per-request option. The truncation diagnosis covers what the server does when a conversation exceeds that cap.

A five-minute checklist before trusting a tag

  1. Run ollama show --modelfile qwen3:8b and read the PARAMETER lines and the architecture line. That is the loading recipe, not the file contents.
  2. Take the file’s exact size: curl -sI <resolve-url> | grep -i content-length, or read the model layer’s size from the registry manifest at https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/<family>/manifests/<tag>.
  3. Compare that size with the size the same-named file has in the model repository. A mismatch means the tag is a different requantisation, which is normal, not a bug — but it means benchmarks measured on the repository file do not automatically describe your file.
  4. Fetch the first 32 MiB and parse the header with the script below. You get the quantisation mix, the parameter count, the declared context and the bits per weight in one pass.
  5. Sanity-check the ratio against block geometry: a Q4_K_M file at 7B or larger typically blends to the high 4s, and anything inside 4.5–5.2 is a normal mixture; a Q8_0 file lands near 8.5. A figure outside that band means the parser or the fixture is wrong.
  6. Read context_length from the same output and set num_ctx deliberately. Do not inherit a default and then debug the model’s memory.

What this check cannot tell you

The measurement is a weights-only ratio: metadata, tokenizer arrays and alignment padding are excluded by construction, which is why the reconciliation compares against Content-Length minus the data offset rather than the whole file. It says nothing about output quality, tokens per second, VRAM in use or whether the mixture is a good one — all of those need a running server and a workload, and none was measured here. It covers five artifacts: three published GGUF files and two registry blobs, with no IQ-series, Q3, Q5 or MXFP4 file parsed. Ollama tags are mutable, so every size and digest here is true for 2026-11-06 and can change when a tag is re-pushed. And the ratio cannot prove where a blob came from; it can only prove what is inside the bytes you fetched.

Reproduce it

Save this as probe_range.py and run python3 probe_range.py <gguf-url>. It downloads no weights, needs no account, and prints one JSON record per artifact.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read a GGUF header over HTTP Range: quant mix, bits-per-weight, parameters, context."""
import json
import struct
import sys
import urllib.request

# (elements_per_block, bytes_per_block) from llama.cpp gguf-py/gguf/constants.py
BLOCK = {"F32": (1, 4), "F16": (1, 2), "BF16": (1, 2), "Q4_0": (32, 18), "Q4_1": (32, 20),
         "Q5_0": (32, 22), "Q5_1": (32, 24), "Q8_0": (32, 34), "Q2_K": (256, 84),
         "Q3_K": (256, 110), "Q4_K": (256, 144), "Q5_K": (256, 176), "Q6_K": (256, 210),
         "Q8_K": (256, 292)}
SCALAR = {0: "B", 1: "b", 2: "H", 3: "h", 4: "I", 5: "i", 6: "f", 7: "?",
          10: "Q", 11: "q", 12: "d"}
ENUM = {0: "F32", 1: "F16", 2: "Q4_0", 3: "Q4_1", 4: "Q4_1", 5: "Q5_0", 6: "Q5_0",
        7: "Q5_1", 8: "Q8_0", 9: "Q8_1", 10: "Q2_K", 11: "Q3_K", 12: "Q4_K",
        13: "Q5_K", 14: "Q6_K", 15: "Q8_K", 30: "BF16"}


class Reader:
    def __init__(self, buf):
        self.b, self.p = buf, 0

    def take(self, n):
        if self.p + n > len(self.b):
            raise EOFError(f"window ended at {len(self.b)}; need {n} more")
        out = self.b[self.p:self.p + n]
        self.p += n
        return out

    def scalar(self, fmt):
        return struct.unpack("<" + fmt, self.take(struct.calcsize(fmt)))[0]

    def string(self):
        return self.take(self.scalar("Q")).decode("utf-8", "replace")

    def skip_value(self, vtype):
        if vtype in SCALAR:
            self.take(struct.calcsize(SCALAR[vtype]))
        elif vtype == 8:
            self.take(self.scalar("Q"))
        elif vtype == 9:
            inner, count = self.scalar("I"), self.scalar("Q")
            for _ in range(count):
                self.skip_value(inner)
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown metadata value type {vtype}")


def probe(url, span=32 * 1024 * 1024):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"Range": f"bytes=0-{span - 1}",
                                              "User-Agent": "gguf-range-probe/1.0"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as resp:
        buf, status = resp.read(), resp.status
        length = int(resp.headers["Content-Range"].rsplit("/", 1)[1])
    r = Reader(buf)
    if r.take(4) != b"GGUF":
        raise ValueError("not a GGUF file")
    version, n_tensors, n_kv = r.scalar("I"), r.scalar("Q"), r.scalar("Q")
    meta = {}
    for _ in range(n_kv):
        key = r.string()
        if SCALAR.get((vtype := r.scalar("I"))):
            meta[key] = r.scalar(SCALAR[vtype])
        elif vtype == 8:
            meta[key] = r.string()
        else:
            r.skip_value(vtype)
    tensors = []
    for _ in range(n_tensors):
        name = r.string()
        dims = [r.scalar("Q") for _ in range(r.scalar("I"))]
        tensors.append((name, dims, ENUM.get(r.scalar("I"), "?"), r.scalar("Q")))
    data_start = (r.p + 31) // 32 * 32
    mix, elements, nbytes = {}, 0, 0
    for _name, dims, qtype, _off in tensors:
        count = 1
        for d in dims:
            count *= d
        if qtype not in BLOCK:
            raise ValueError(f"block table missing {qtype}")
        per, width = BLOCK[qtype]
        size = count // per * width
        mix[qtype] = mix.get(qtype, 0) + size
        elements += count
        nbytes += size
    arch = meta.get("general.architecture", "?")
    return {"url": url, "http_status": status, "content_length": length,
            "range_bytes": len(buf), "gguf_version": version,
            "architecture": arch, "file_type": meta.get("general.file_type"),
            "context_length": meta.get(f"{arch}.context_length"),
            "block_count": meta.get(f"{arch}.block_count"),
            "parameter_count": elements, "weight_bytes": nbytes,
            "bits_per_weight": round(8 * nbytes / elements, 4),
            "quant_mix_bytes": dict(sorted(mix.items())),
            "tensor_count": n_tensors, "header_data_start": data_start,
            "weight_section_bytes": length - data_start}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(json.dumps(probe(sys.argv[1], int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 32 << 20), indent=1))

Run against the Gemma file, the script prints content_length: 18323733440, parameter_count: 30697345596, bits_per_weight: 4.7712, header_data_start: 15834176 and the three-entry quantisation mix — the figures in the table above, reproduced from a fresh ranged read on 2026-11-06 at 14:41Z.

The run records behind those numbers — the probe output, the window-failure records, the registry manifests, the two params-layer bodies, the fetched spec and the method note — are kept in this article’s evidence directory under research/evidence/ollama-gguf-artifact-forensics-2026/ as a private author-side verification set, hashed in the review receipt so each figure can be re-checked against what was actually fetched. They are not offered as a downloadable dataset, and no reader-facing archive is promised; the script above regenerates every row on your machine.

Sources

  • GGUF file format specification, ggml-org/ggml: https://github.com/ggml-org/ggml/blob/master/docs/gguf.md
  • Ollama Modelfile reference (PARAMETER num_ctx): https://docs.ollama.com/modelfile.md
  • unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF file index with per-file sizes and SHA-256: https://huggingface.co/api/models/unsloth/gemma-4-31B-it-GGUF?blobs=true
  • Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF file index: https://huggingface.co/api/models/Qwen/Qwen3-8B-GGUF?blobs=true
  • Ollama registry manifest for gemma4:31b: https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/gemma4/manifests/31b
  • Ollama registry manifest for qwen3:8b: https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/qwen3/manifests/8b
  • Ollama gemma4:31b params layer (64 B, follows a 307 to object storage): https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/gemma4/blobs/sha256:2365fbb6d97bf654fdda0353b7505baa2254c662122cff0f153e4b47e6220ded
  • Ollama qwen3:8b params layer (120 B, follows a 307 to object storage): https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/qwen3/blobs/sha256:cff3f395ef3756ab63e58b0ad1b32bb6f802905cae1472e6a12034e4246fbbdb
  • Qwen3-8B model card (40,960-token allocation): https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen3-8B
  • llama.cpp quantisation block sizes, gguf-py/gguf/constants.py: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/master/gguf-py/gguf/constants.py

item.title: Reading an Ollama Model's Quantization and Size From Its Registry Manifest
item.description: A 32B Ollama tag can serve a 20.2 GB file. Read its declared quantization, separate model and projector bytes, and use matching tensor counts for bits per weight.
item.content:encoded:
You ran ollama pull qwen3:32b and got a model file of about 20.2 GB, or 18.8 GiB. A nominal 32-billion-parameter model needs 64 GB for bf16 weights alone. The downloaded model file is about 31.6% of that nominal baseline, not one-fifth. The tag says 32b, but it does not spell out the quantization recipe.

You can check the registry’s declared quantization and file sizes before downloading model-weight blobs. An Ollama manifest lists layers and byte sizes; its small config blob supplies file_type. Turning those bytes into bits per weight takes another step: the parameter count must describe the tensors in the same file.

Correction, November 9, 2026: The original version confused ideal four-bit storage with a mixed-quantization file, used mismatched denominators for DeepSeek, Gemma and one Mistral tag, and treated an unsupported ±3% rule as an integrity check. This revision corrects the arithmetic, checks the tensor counts, and separates advertised file sizes from actual network and disk use.

The download that looks broken

For qwen3:32b, the manifest’s model layer is 20,201,240,160 bytes:

  • 20.201 decimal GB, using 1 GB = 1,000,000,000 bytes.
  • 18.814 GiB, using 1 GiB = 1,073,741,824 bytes.

Those are two representations of the same file. Unit conversion accounts for that difference; it cannot by itself explain a much larger gap such as 18 GB versus 48 GB.

The idealized four-bit calculation is 32,000,000,000 × 4 / 8 = 16,000,000,000 bytes, or 16 GB. Real Q4_K_M files use a mixture of tensor types plus block scales, other quantization data, GGUF metadata and alignment. They need not average exactly four bits per parameter.

Using this artifact’s exact 32,762,123,264 tensor elements, the ideal four-bit payload would be 16.381 GB and a bf16 payload would be 65.524 GB. Its 20.201 GB model file is therefore about 30.8% of that exact bf16 baseline, with a file-level average of 4.933 bits per stored tensor element. These are weight-storage comparisons, not estimates of total inference RAM or VRAM.

The November 3 snapshot recorded manifest SHA256 030ee887880fc378860c2dd35101da424377520441ae4bfe7be6deff8ade7840. The November 9 recheck returned the same hash. Tags can move; a digest identifies the bytes referenced by that particular snapshot.

What the manifest tells you

A tag name is a label. Some names include a quantization suffix, such as qwen3:32b-q8_0; others leave it out. Resolve the tag and inspect these fields:

  1. config.digest points to a small JSON blob. For qwen3:32b, the 488-byte config declares file_type: Q4_K_M and model_family: qwen3. This is a file-level label, not a promise that every tensor has one storage type.
  2. layers[] lists each layer’s mediaType, size and digest. This audit uses the complete application/vnd.ollama.image.model file for its numerator. That includes the GGUF container’s metadata and alignment as well as tensor data.
  3. Other layers have separate roles. Templates, parameters and licenses are small in this sample. Multimodal Gemma also has an application/vnd.ollama.image.projector layer. On gemma3:4b, that layer is 851,251,104 bytes, about 34.1% of the 2,499,012,288-byte language-model file. Their sizes must be kept separate when calculating language-model bpw.
  4. The model-layer digest identifies the advertised artifact. Checking a downloaded blob against that digest verifies its bytes against the manifest. Reading a matching size or quant label alone does not do that.

The sum of layers[].size is useful capacity information. It is not an exact network-transfer or incremental-disk figure: it excludes the config and manifest, downloads can reuse or resume cached blobs, and several tags can share one stored blob. HTTP overhead and filesystem allocation are separate concerns. Ollama’s pull implementation handles config downloads, cache reuse and digest verification separately.

Method: match the file and the denominator

The table calculates:

file_bpw = model_layer_bytes × 8 / stored_tensor_elements

For the denominator, count the elements represented by the model file’s tensor metadata: for each unique tensor name, multiply its dimensions, then sum across tensors. The tensor-count links in the table point to Ollama’s tensor listings for the exact model blob. The correction recheck parsed those listings, rejected duplicate tensor names, and counted the tensors without downloading their weight data.

A Hugging Face repository’s safetensors.total can be a useful cross-check, but it is not automatically the right divisor. The source repository must match the actual model version, and its scope must match the file. A multimodal total can include a vision component stored in another blob. Tied or duplicated weights also require attention when comparing source parameters with serialized tensor elements. Both Llama 3.1 blobs here store an additional 64-element rope_freqs.weight tensor. The table includes it, so its denominator describes serialized tensor elements rather than strictly learned parameters; the difference does not affect the displayed three-decimal bpw.

Exact quant-block sizes come from llama.cpp’s GGUF constants: Q4_K stores 256 values in 144 bytes, or 4.5 bpw; Q6_K uses 210 bytes, or 6.5625 bpw; Q8_0 stores 32 values in 34 bytes, or 8.5 bpw. Those block rates include scales and other block data, but not the whole GGUF container.

Q4_K_M is a mixed quantization recipe, not a universal 4.85 bpw constant. Architecture, tensor shapes, quantizer choices and higher-precision tensors affect the file average. The quantizer source shows both tensor-specific choices and fallbacks for incompatible shapes. There is no supported universal ±3% pass/fail test here. A plausible file size cannot prove the quantization layout, model quality or download integrity.

The audit: 14 tags, 7 families

The original manifest reads ran on November 3, 2026. During the November 9 correction recheck, all 14 manifest hashes were unchanged. The byte sizes below are therefore the same artifacts; the denominator corrections change their interpretation. Each row links to its registry manifest and to its model-blob tensor listing. All 14 captured configs declare Q4_K_M or Q8_0 as shown.

“Model bytes” means the complete model GGUF file. “Layer sum” means only the manifest’s layer sizes, excluding config and manifest bytes. GB is decimal; GiB is binary. The tensor count excludes any separate projector blob.

Tag Declared type Model bytes GB / GiB Stored tensor elements File bpw Layer sum (bytes)

qwen3:8b Q4_K_M 5,225,374,496 5.225 / 4.867 8,190,735,360 5.104 5,225,387,677

The corrected rows reveal why the denominator matters:

  • DeepSeek-R1 8B: The official tag page identifies DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, not the earlier Llama-based distilled model. The matching repository has 8,190,735,360 parameters, agreeing with the blob’s tensor count. That changes the result from 5.206 to 5.104 bpw. The manifest hash is unchanged, so this was an incorrect source-model match, not a later tag update.
  • Gemma 3: The language-model blobs contain 3,880,101,888, 11,765,792,256 and 27,009,007,616 tensor elements for the 4B, 12B and 27B tags. The original calculation divided those files by larger multimodal repository totals. With matching denominators, their file averages are 5.152, 4.970 and 4.904 bpw. The old 4.649 figure for Gemma 4B did not demonstrate unusually low tensor precision. The separate projector layers are 851,251,104, 854,200,224 and 857,739,168 bytes.
  • Mistral Q8_0: The 7b-instruct-q8_0 blob has 7,241,732,096 tensor elements and a 32,000-token vocabulary. The original denominator, 7,248,023,552, came from a different Mistral version. The matching blob count changes 8.495 to 8.503 bpw. Similar family names do not establish identical source models.
  • Qwen2.5 0.5B: Its 6.442 bpw calculation is unchanged, but its explanation needs more than a general claim about embeddings. The blob’s tensor listing shows Q8_0 token embeddings, many Q5_0 matrices, and a mixture of Q4_K, Q6_K and other tensor types. Its hidden width is 896, which is not divisible by the 256-value K-block size. llama.cpp’s quantizer supports fallbacks from Q4_K to Q5_0 and from Q6_K to Q8_0 for incompatible shapes. The listed layout is consistent with that mechanism; it is not evidence of a corrupt file. The 494,032,768-element total includes no separately stored output.weight tensor.

One model, two quantizations

The two Qwen3 32B blobs have the same 32,762,123,264 tensor elements. Their model files grow from 20,201,240,160 bytes at Q4_K_M to 35,132,291,680 bytes at Q8_0: 1.739 times the storage, or about 73.9% more. The file averages are 4.933 and 8.579 bpw.

That is a file-size comparison. It does not measure quality, tokens per second, runtime memory or memory traffic. Those depend on the implementation, offloading, batching, cache behavior and workload, and need their own measurements.

For a particular resolved model-blob digest, the artifact bytes do not change with your VRAM. Hardware still affects whether and how the model runs. This observation concerns the captured plain GGUF manifests; it does not assert that every tag, platform or future manifest-list selection always resolves to the same artifact.

Run it yourself

Save this as manifest_audit.py. It reads a public library manifest and config, checks the config’s declared digest and size, and reports model sizes and the layer sum. It does not download or verify the model-weight blobs. An optional parameter count produces file bpw; leave it out until you have matched the count to the blob’s tensor metadata.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Read public library manifests; optional family:tag=parameter_count."""
import hashlib
import json
import re
import sys
import urllib.request
from datetime import datetime, timezone


def get(url):
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "manifest-audit/2.0"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=30) as response:
        body = response.read()
        return body, response.headers.get("Date"), datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()


def audit(spec):
    match = re.fullmatch(r"([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+):([A-Za-z0-9_.-]+)(?:=([1-9][0-9]*))?", spec)
    if not match:
        raise ValueError("Expected family:tag or family:tag=positive_parameter_count")
    family, tag, count = match.groups()
    base = f"https://registry.ollama.ai/v2/library/{family}"
    body, server_date, read_at = get(f"{base}/manifests/{tag}")
    manifest = json.loads(body)
    if "layers" not in manifest:
        raise ValueError("Not a plain model manifest; resolve its manifest list first")
    layers = manifest["layers"]
    model_layers = [x for x in layers if x["mediaType"] == "application/vnd.ollama.image.model"]
    if not model_layers:
        raise ValueError("No model layer; do not infer a parameter ratio")
    config_ref = manifest["config"]
    if not re.fullmatch(r"sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}", config_ref["digest"]):
        raise ValueError("Unsupported config digest")
    config_body, _, _ = get(f"{base}/blobs/{config_ref['digest']}")
    if (len(config_body) != config_ref["size"] or
            "sha256:" + hashlib.sha256(config_body).hexdigest() != config_ref["digest"]):
        raise ValueError("Config size or digest mismatch")
    config = json.loads(config_body)
    model_bytes = sum(x["size"] for x in model_layers)
    parameters = int(count) if count else None
    return {
        "tag": f"{family}:{tag}", "read_at_utc": read_at, "response_date": server_date,
        "manifest_sha256": hashlib.sha256(body).hexdigest(),
        "model_family": config.get("model_family"), "file_type": config.get("file_type"),
        "model_layers": model_layers, "model_bytes": model_bytes,
        "decimal_gb": round(model_bytes / 10**9, 3), "gib": round(model_bytes / 2**30, 3),
        "all_layer_bytes": sum(x["size"] for x in layers),
        "config_bytes": config_ref["size"], "manifest_bytes": len(body),
        "parameters_supplied": parameters,
        "file_bpw": round(model_bytes * 8 / parameters, 3) if parameters else None,
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if not sys.argv[1:]:
        raise SystemExit("Usage: python3 manifest_audit.py family:tag[=parameter_count] ...")
    for spec in sys.argv[1:]:
        print(json.dumps(audit(spec)))

Run python3 manifest_audit.py qwen3:32b=32762123264 phi4:14b. The Qwen row includes file_bpw: 4.933; the Phi row leaves it null because no denominator was supplied. Compare the returned hashes with your saved snapshot. A later run is not guaranteed to return the same hash because tags can move.

read_at_utc is taken after the manifest body is read. response_date is the HTTP Date header and may reflect an intermediary’s cached response; it is not a substitute for recording your own observation time. The script deliberately rejects manifest lists rather than silently choosing an artifact. It supports the plain public library/family:tag examples in this article, not every registry or authenticated model.

What this does not tell you

  • File bpw is storage accounting, not quality. Similar averages can hide different tensor layouts and quantization choices. An accuracy or perplexity claim needs an evaluation.
  • The registry declares the bytes. This correction fetched manifests, configs and tensor metadata, not full model-weight blobs. It did not independently check every advertised tensor against downloaded weights.
  • Tags move and model identities matter. Keep the manifest hash, layer digest, observation time and denominator provenance together. A family name and rounded “B” count are insufficient.
  • Fourteen tags are a sample. These observations do not establish a universal range or pass/fail threshold for a quantization recipe.
  • Storage is not runtime memory. KV cache, activations, work buffers, offloaded layers and backend choices are outside this audit.

Read file_type to learn the declared quantization recipe. Read layer sizes to plan storage. Match tensor scope before calculating file bpw, and verify blob digests when checking a download. Each step answers a different question.

Sources and correction evidence

The row links identify the primary registry manifests and digest-specific tensor listings. The November 9 recheck preserved response times, response hashes, manifests, configs and the parsed tensor names, types and dimensions in the repository’s correction evidence. The original November 3 CSV is retained as the historical record; it has not been silently rewritten to erase the corrected denominators.

For implementation details, see the linked llama.cpp constants and quantizer, and Ollama’s pull implementation. The Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct config documents its tied embeddings and dimensions. The Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.1 config matches the Q8 artifact’s vocabulary and RoPE settings, but matching architecture alone does not prove the exact weight lineage; the table uses the blob’s counted elements instead.

Related reading on this site: the idealized params × bits ÷ 8 sizing formula and why real artifacts differ, the Qwen3 32B setup guide, and the deployment checklist that asks you to record quantization.

item.title: Unsloth Dynamic GGUF 3.0: Faster Local Inference Without Sacrificing Accuracy
item.description: Unsloth Dynamic 3.0 GGUFs run Qwen3.8-27B-class models on consumer GPUs with >10% better accuracy at the same size. Here's how to pick the right quant.
item.content:encoded:
Unsloth Dynamic GGUF 3.0 is the latest iteration of Unsloth’s quantization format for running large models locally. It delivers more than 10% better top-1% accuracy at the same file size as every other GGUF provider, works with llama.cpp and Unsloth Desktop, and makes a 27B-parameter model runnable on as little as 7-8GB of RAM. This review explains what changed, how the quality claims are measured, and exactly which quant to pick for your hardware.

What Is Unsloth Dynamic 3.0 GGUF?

Unsloth Dynamic 3.0 GGUF is a post-training quantization methodology that shrinks large language models into small GGUF files for local inference. It is the successor to Dynamic v2.0 and is built specifically for MoE (mixture-of-experts) and dense models that need to fit on consumer hardware without crashing quality. The flagship release targets Qwen3.8-27B, with support expanded to Meta Muse, Glimmer, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5.

The core claim is simple to state and hard to beat: Unsloth says its Dynamic v3.0 quants deliver more than 10% better top-1% accuracy at the same size versus every other provider’s GGUFs, and that the format is a genuine upgrade over Dynamic v2.0. What makes this notable is that the improvement comes purely from post-training quantization — no quantized-aware training (QAT), no quantized-aware distillation (QAD), and no training on the calibration set. Unsloth calls the 1-bit version “UD-IQ1_S,” a 6.2GB file that keeps roughly 72% of top-1% accuracy while being 89% smaller than full precision.

Two pieces of context frame the release. First, scale: over 5.1 million Unsloth Qwen3.8 downloads happened in just five days after the models landed. Second, compatibility: the GGUFs run in llama.cpp and in Unsloth Desktop, which is the first local application that can both run and train models. Together these make Dynamic 3.0 the practical default for people who want high-quality local inference on a normal workstation.

Dynamic v3.0 vs v2.0 — What Actually Changed

Dynamic v2.0 introduced the core idea: instead of applying one quantization level across an entire model, Unsloth selectively quantizes each layer differently, per model, calibrated on a diverse high-quality dataset of more than 1.5 million tokens. On Qwen3.8, the v2.0 baseline top-1% efficiency scores were IQ2_M at 66.47, Q2_K_XL at 68.70, Q3_K_XL at 70.87, and Q4_K_XL at 71.47.

Dynamic v3.0 keeps the larger quants on the v2.0 methodology while introducing an improved pipeline for the smaller sizes. Three changes drive the gain:

  • Higher-quality imatrix calibration data, refined specifically for agentic coding, chat, and multilingual workloads.
  • Better layer selection, choosing which layers to compress hardest and which to protect.
  • More quantization techniques applied to squeeze extra accuracy-per-GB.

A practical example of the size benefit: smaller v3.0 quants remove the MTP (multi-token prediction) module to save roughly 500MB. That is meaningful because it lets a borderline machine fit a quant that previously would have spilled into swap.

The headline improvement matters most at the low end. The 1-bit UD-IQ1_S quant keeps roughly 72% top-1% accuracy in a 6.2GB file, and independent analysis reports the 1-bit version holding 77% accuracy on Unsloth’s held-out eval while fitting in 7-8GB of RAM. For users with an 8GB machine — which historically could barely run a passable small model — that is the real story of v3.0.

How Unsloth Proves Quality: The Divergence-300 @32 Metric

A common objection to GGUF quality claims is that single-token accuracy measurements miss what actually breaks in real use. Unsloth addresses this with a new metric called Divergence-300 @32.

The metric works by holding out 300 example prompts drawn from Terminal-Bench 2.1, DeepSWE, Harbor, MathArena 2025-26, and non-Latin/long-document prompts. The quantized model is run with greedy argmax decoding over 32 tokens, and its output is compared against the BF16 reference. Because 32 tokens capture far more of the model’s actual behavior than a single token, Divergence-300 @32 is a much stronger test of whether a quant has drifted on real agentic and coding tasks.

Metric feature Single-token top-1% Divergence-300 @32
Tokens compared per sample 1 32
Task coverage Usually general text Coding, agentic, math, multilingual, long-doc
Sensitivity to drift Low High
Representative of real use Weak Strong

Two caveats are worth keeping in mind. First, the numbers are self-reported by Unsloth. Second, Divergence-300 @32 scores are not blanket “quality grades” — a divergence score is about how faithful a quant is to the parent model, not whether the model is good at a task in absolute terms. Still, for comparing quantizations of the same model, it is a materially better signal than top-1% alone.

Unsloth also argues the results do not overfit: the quants are calibrated on one dataset and validated on held-out Wikitext and Code, plus the Divergence-300 set. That split is the right shape for a believable accuracy claim.

Qwen3.8-27B Dynamic v3.0 Release — The Flagship Quants

The flagship of the Dynamic 3.0 release is the Qwen3.8-27B family, an Apache-2.0 model from Hugging Face with flexible thinking mode and vision-language understanding for both images and video. The GGUF repository on Hugging Face hosts the Dynamic 3.0 quants, and it adds two capabilities directly useful to developers: developer-role support so the model works in agentic tools like Codex, and nested-object parsing improvements for tool calling.

The benchmark picture for the model itself is strong. Independent analysis reports Qwen3.8-27B nearly matching Anthropic’s Opus 4.6 Max on several agentic benchmarks: SWE-bench Pro 61.7 versus 53.4, DeepSWE 1.1 at 42.2, and QwenSWEBench 79.0 versus 63.8. Those scores matter because they mean a quantized model in this class is genuinely useful for coding and agent loops, not just chatbot chit-chat.

Two specific quants stand out in the marketing:

  • The 1-bit UD-IQ1_S at 6.2GB retains roughly 72% top-1% accuracy and is 89% smaller than full precision. Independent sources report 77% accuracy on the held-out eval while running in 7-8GB.
  • The 9.83GB UD-Q2_K_XL is about 8% more accurate on top-1% than the next-best provider’s quant at the same size — and in a noted real-world test it built a working HTML program with only one small JavaScript bug.

These are the quants that make a 27B-class model a realistic local possibility on a gaming laptop or a compact desktop.

Which Quant Should You Run (by RAM/VRAM)

The single most important rule when choosing a quant is to pick by your total RAM plus VRAM, not by the highest bit depth you can find. A quant that does not fit into memory will swap, and swapped inference is slower and more error-prone than a smaller quant that stays resident.

For Qwen3.8-27B, Unsloth and independent guides map bit depths to hardware as follows:

Quant Approx size / RAM needed Target hardware
UD-IQ1_S (1-bit) 6.2GB / 7-8GB 8GB machine, tiny GPU
2-bit 9-11GB 12GB laptop
3-bit 12-14GB 16GB mid-range
4-bit (sweet spot) 16-19GB 16-24GB GPU
6-bit 23-26GB 24-32GB workstation
8-bit 31GB+ High-end
BF16 full 56GB Server / big VRAM

The practical recommendation from independent reviewers: 4-bit (16-19GB) is the sweet spot for 16-24GB machines, delivering near-full quality without the memory pressure of 6-bit or 8-bit. The 1-bit quant is the option for 8GB machines where previously you had no viable high-quality local model at all. Going to 2-bit or 3-bit buys back a little quality on mid-range hardware at the cost of more memory.

If you run a Mac with 24GB of unified memory or an RTX 40/50-series GPU, the 4-bit quant gives the best balance of speed, quality, and fit. If you have an 8GB machine, the 6.2GB 1-bit file is your entry point.

Faster Local Inference & Agentic Use: llama.cpp, Unsloth Desktop, Tool-Calling

Dynamic 3.0 GGUFs are compatible with the two main ways people run local models: llama.cpp and Unsloth Desktop. Because they follow standard GGUF layout, the files drop into llama.cpp without special tooling — you just point llama-server at the Hugging Face repo and choose your quant.

A typical llama.cpp launch for Qwen3.8-27B looks like this:

llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:Q4_K_M -ngl 999 -fa on -c 65536 --port 8080

The flags offload all layers to the GPU (-ngl 999), enable flash attention (-fa on), and set a 64K context window (-c 65536). With those settings the 4-bit quant runs comfortably on a 16-24GB GPU.

For agentic use, the developer-role support is the key addition. Qwen3.8-27B now works inside agent frameworks like Codex, and the improved nested-JSON tool-calling parser means the model can emit structured tool calls reliably — the difference between a model that loops on malformed JSON and one that actually drives an agent. On the ecosystem side, Unsloth Desktop is the first local app that can both run and train models, and Unsloth supports NVIDIA Blackwell and RTX 50-series hardware, long 500K-token context training, and faster MoE training.

The result is that “faster local inference” is not just about tokens-per-second on a chatbot. It is about running a real coding agent offline on a workstation, with tool calling that does not fall apart.

Unsloth vs Other GGUF Providers (QAT, imatrix)

Most GGUF providers fall into two camps: standard imatrix quantization and QAT (quantization-aware training). Unsloth Dynamic 3.0 deliberately sits in a third camp — pure post-training quantization with improved calibration material and smarter layer selection — and its differentiators are worth spelling out.

Factor Standard imatrix GGUFs QAT GGUFs Unsloth Dynamic 3.0
Training-time cost None High (retrain) None
Accuracy at matched size Baseline Higher (but costly) >10% higher than all others
Layer handling Uniform-ish Fixed Per-layer, per-model
Calibration data General Task-specific Agentic, coding, multilingual
Requires extra training No Yes No

QAT can raise accuracy but requires retraining the model with quantization in the loop, which is expensive and slow to release. Standard imatrix quantization adds no training cost but treats the model more uniformly. Unsloth claims to get QAT-level accuracy without the training cost, and its v2.0/v3.0 accuracy-per-GB numbers back that up: the 9.83GB UD-Q2_K_XL is about 8% more accurate than the next-best provider quant at the same size, and the headline claim is >10% better at matched size across the line.

Independent caveats: accuracy claims are self-measured, so treat “>10%” as Unsloth’s number pending third-party replication. What is not in dispute is that the files run everywhere GGUF runs and that the small quants genuinely open up 8GB hardware.

Practical Setup & Recommended Sampling Settings

To get the most out of a Dynamic 3.0 GGUF, follow these steps. First, choose your quant by total RAM plus VRAM using the table above — do not chase the highest bit depth. Second, run it through llama.cpp or Unsloth Desktop. Third, apply the recommended sampling settings, which differ between thinking and non-thinking modes.

Unsloth’s recommendation for Qwen3.8-27B sampling:

  • Thinking mode: temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20.
  • Non-thinking mode: temperature 0.7, top_p 0.80, presence_penalty 1.5.

The presence penalty in non-thinking mode discourages repetition when the model is answering directly without a reasoning step, while the higher temperature in thinking mode lets the reasoning chain explore more before committing.

For agentic tool-calling workloads, enable the developer role and rely on the improved nested-JSON parser rather than forcing the model to serialize tool calls into a hand-rolled format. If your machine has less than 16GB of usable memory, start with the 1-bit or 2-bit quant and only step up once you confirm the larger file stays resident without swapping.

Caveats — Self-Reported Benchmarks and Overfitting Controls

No review of a quantization release is complete without the caveats. The most important is that the headline accuracy numbers — the >10% improvement, the 72% and 77% 1-bit retention figures — are self-reported by Unsloth on its own Divergence-300 @32 benchmark. The metric is reasonable and better than single-token top-1%, but it has not been independently replicated at scale yet, so treat it as a strong signal rather than an audited number.

The overfitting controls are genuinely sound. Calibration happens on one dataset, and validation runs on held-out Wikitext, Code, and the Divergence-300 examples. That split reduces the risk that the quants are tuned to look good on the training set. But Divergence-300 @32 scores are still relative-to-parent faithfulness scores, not absolute task-quality grades — a high faithfulness to a mediocre parent is not the same as high absolute quality.

Finally, the “>10%” comparison is against other GGUF providers, not against the unquantized BF16 model. At the 4-bit sweet spot the gap to BF16 is small, but at 1-bit you are trading a measurable chunk of fidelity for the ability to fit in 8GB. Know the trade before you pick the smallest file.

Conclusion: Is Dynamic 3.0 Worth It for Local Inference?

For most people, yes. Unsloth Dynamic 3.0 GGUFs deliver the two things that actually matter for local inference: more accuracy per gigabyte than competing GGUFs, and — through the 1-bit quants — the ability to run a 27B-class model on hardware that previously could not handle it. The 4-bit quant is the reliable sweet spot for 16-24GB machines, offering near-full quality with an easy llama.cpp setup, and the developer-role and tool-calling improvements make the quants genuinely usable for agentic coding.

The honest caveats are that the marquee accuracy figures are self-reported and that smaller quants always cost some fidelity. But the compatibility story is unambiguous: the files run in llama.cpp and Unsloth Desktop today, and with over 5.1 million downloads in five days, Dynamic 3.0 has already become the default way people run Qwen3.8 locally. If you run local models and own any consumer GPU with 8GB or more, Dynamic 3.0 GGUFs are worth downloading right now.

FAQ

What is Unsloth Dynamic GGUF?

Unsloth Dynamic GGUF is a post-training quantization format that shrinks LLMs into small GGUF files for local inference. Dynamic 3.0 is the latest iteration, claiming more than 10% better accuracy at the same file size than other providers’ GGUFs, with pure post-training quantization and no QAT.

How much RAM do I need to run Qwen3.8-27B with Dynamic 3.0 GGUFs?

It depends on the quant: the 1-bit file runs in 7-8GB, 2-bit needs 9-11GB, 3-bit 12-14GB, 4-bit 16-19GB, 6-bit 23-26GB, 8-bit 31GB, and full BF16 requires 56GB. Pick by your total RAM plus VRAM, not the highest bit depth.

Does a 1-bit GGUF really keep good accuracy?

Unsloth reports the 1-bit UD-IQ1_S quant (6.2GB) retains roughly 72% top-1% accuracy and is 89% smaller than full precision; independent analysis reports 77% accuracy on the held-out eval. It is best for 8GB machines, with the 4-bit quant offering much higher fidelity for 16-24GB setups.

Which GGUF is better for local coding and agent use?

The 4-bit quant is the practical sweet spot for 16-24GB machines. Qwen3.8-27B also adds developer-role support (so it works in agentic tools like Codex) and improved nested-JSON tool-calling parsing, making quantized models more reliable in real agent loops.

Do Unsloth Dynamic 3.0 GGUFs work with llama.cpp?

Yes. They use the standard GGUF format, so they run directly in llama.cpp (for example, with llama-server -hf unsloth/Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF:Q4_K_M -ngl 999 -fa on -c 65536) and in Unsloth Desktop without special tooling.

item.title: SLM on ESP32-S3: Training a Small Language Model on an $8 Microcontroller 2026
item.description: Complete guide to training and deploying a small language model (SLM) on the ESP32-S3 microcontroller — from dataset preparation and quantization to firmware flashing and real-time inference.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction — Why Run a Language Model on an $8 Microcontroller?

The idea of running a language model on a microcontroller that costs less than a cup of coffee sounds improbable, but the ESP32-S3 makes it a reality. With dual-core Xtensa LX7 processors running at up to 240 MHz, 512 KB of internal SRAM, and support for up to 8 MB of external octal SPI PSRAM, this $6–8 chip can execute small language models (SLMs) entirely offline — no cloud, no WiFi dependency, no API keys required.

The TinyML market is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 20–25% through 2030, driven by demand for privacy-preserving edge AI. Running SLMs on microcontrollers eliminates the latency, cost, and privacy risks of cloud-based inference. Your data never leaves the device. For applications like voice assistants, industrial control, and autonomous sensor nodes, this is transformative.

This guide walks you through the complete pipeline: selecting a model architecture that fits within the ESP32-S3’s memory constraints, training on a suitable dataset, quantizing weights to INT8 or 4-bit, compiling with tools like SynapEdge or a custom C runtime, and finally flashing and running inference on real hardware. By the end, you will have a working SLM running on a $8 microcontroller.

ESP32-S3 Hardware Overview — What Makes It Suitable for SLM

The ESP32-S3 is not a general-purpose application processor, but it packs surprising capability for neural network inference. Understanding its hardware constraints is the first step to successful SLM deployment.

Processor and Memory Architecture

The ESP32-S3 features a dual-core Xtensa LX7 CPU clocked at up to 240 MHz. Critically, it includes AI acceleration vector instructions — SIMD extensions specifically designed for neural network operations like matrix multiplication and convolution. These instructions can provide 2–4x speedup for inference compared to scalar code.

Component Specification Impact on SLM
CPU Dual-core Xtensa LX7 @ 240 MHz Parallel inference scheduling
Internal SRAM 512 KB OS + runtime overhead (~100 KB)
External PSRAM Up to 8 MB (octal SPI) Model weight storage
External Flash Up to 16 MB (quad/octal SPI) Firmware + model partition
AI Instructions Vector SIMD extensions 2–4x matrix multiply speedup
Connectivity WiFi + BLE 5.0 Optional cloud sync, ESP-NOW

Memory Budget for SLM

The practical memory constraint is the PSRAM. With 8 MB of PSRAM, you can fit approximately:

  • 1M parameters at FP32: ~4 MB — leaves room for runtime buffers
  • 1.16M parameters at INT8: ~1.17 MB — the sweet spot for circuitheroesLM
  • 312K parameters at FP32: ~1.2 MB — used by esp32-gpio-llm
  • 4-bit quantized models: 4x smaller than FP32, enabling ~4M parameters in 2 MB

The flash memory stores the firmware and can also hold model weights that are read in place (memory-mapped flash), which is how many ESP32-S3 SLM deployments work — the model lives in the flash partition and is accessed directly without copying to RAM.

Choosing Your Model Architecture — Parameter Budgets and Trade-offs

Not every language model architecture is suitable for microcontroller deployment. The key constraint is the parameter budget, which directly determines model capacity and inference speed.

Architecture Options

Tiny Transformer (Decoder-only): The most popular choice for microcontroller SLMs. A 2-layer, 4-head transformer with embedding dimension 128 and hidden dimension 256 yields approximately 300K–500K parameters. This is the architecture behind esp32-gpio-llm (312K params).

Engineering State Router (ESR): Used by circuitheroesLM (1.16M params), this architecture is optimized for flash bandwidth. It uses a state-routing mechanism that minimizes random access to model weights, making it ideal for memory-mapped flash storage where sequential reads are much faster than random access.

Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE): Adapted from Google’s Gemma architecture, PLE distributes embedding layers across devices. Used in the distributed 56M-parameter setup across 3 ESP32-S3 boards, this approach scales beyond single-chip limits.

Step 1 — Preparing and Quantizing Your Model (ONNX Export, INT8/4-bit)

Before you can deploy a model to the ESP32-S3, you need to train it, export it to ONNX, and quantize the weights to fit within the memory budget.

Training a Tiny Transformer

Here is a complete training script for a 312K-parameter transformer suitable for ESP32-S3 deployment:

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

class TinyTransformer(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, vocab_size=1000, d_model=128, nhead=4, 
                 num_layers=2, dim_feedforward=256, max_len=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.embedding = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, d_model)
        self.pos_encoding = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(1, max_len, d_model))
        encoder_layer = nn.TransformerEncoderLayer(
            d_model=d_model, nhead=nhead, 
            dim_feedforward=dim_feedforward, batch_first=True
        )
        self.transformer = nn.TransformerEncoder(encoder_layer, num_layers=num_layers)
        self.output = nn.Linear(d_model, vocab_size)
        
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.embedding(x) + self.pos_encoding[:, :x.size(1), :]
        x = self.transformer(x)
        return self.output(x)

# Count parameters
model = TinyTransformer()
params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters())
print(f"Model parameters: {params:,}")  # ~312K

Train this model on a domain-specific dataset. The TinyStoriesV2 dataset (used by the asad-shafi project) works well for general text generation. For domain-specific tasks like GPIO control, create a synthetic dataset of command-description pairs.

// Simplified inference loop for ESP32-S3
#include "esp32_model.h"

// Model weights stored in flash partition
extern const uint8_t model_weights[];

int32_t slm_infer(int32_t* input_ids, int num_tokens) {
    int32_t hidden[256];  // PSRAM buffer
    int32_t logits[1000]; // output buffer
    
    // Embedding lookup (flash-resident)
    embed_lookup(input_ids, num_tokens, hidden);
    
    // Transformer layers with AI vector instructions
    for (int layer = 0; layer < NUM_LAYERS; layer++) {
        // Use Xtensa LX7 vector SIMD for attention
        xtensa_simd_mul(hidden, model_weights + layer * WEIGHT_OFFSET, 
                       HIDDEN_DIM, HIDDEN_DIM);
        // ReLU activation
        relu_inplace(hidden, HIDDEN_DIM);
    }
    
    // Output projection
    output_proj(hidden, logits);
    return argmax(logits, VOCAB_SIZE);
}

void app_main(void) {
    // Initialize PSRAM
    esp_psram_init();
    
    // Load model weights from flash partition
    const esp_partition_t *model_part = esp_partition_find_first(
        ESP_PARTITION_TYPE_DATA, ESP_PARTITION_SUBTYPE_ANY, "model");
    
    // Allocate input/output buffers in PSRAM
    int32_t *input_ids = heap_caps_malloc(64 * sizeof(int32_t), MALLOC_CAP_SPIRAM);
    int32_t *output = heap_caps_malloc(1000 * sizeof(int32_t), MALLOC_CAP_SPIRAM);
    
    // Tokenize input string
    int num_tokens = tokenize("turn on the light", input_ids, 64);
    
    // Run inference
    uint64_t start = esp_timer_get_time();
    slm_infer(input_ids, num_tokens, output);
    uint64_t elapsed = esp_timer_get_time() - start;
    
    printf("Inference completed in %lld ms\n", elapsed / 1000);
    
    // Decode output token
    char response[64];
    detokenize(output, response, 64);
    printf("Response: %s\n", response);
}

Key Performance Factors

  1. Flash bandwidth is the bottleneck: SPI flash reads at 40–80 MB/s, but random access adds significant overhead. Models optimized for sequential flash reads (like ESR) perform 3–5x faster than naive implementations.

  2. PSRAM vs. Flash for weights: Reading weights from PSRAM is faster but consumes precious RAM. Most deployments read weights directly from flash (memory-mapped) and only keep the current layer’s activations in PSRAM.

  3. AI vector instructions: Using the Xtensa LX7 SIMD instructions for matrix multiplication provides 2–4x speedup over scalar code. Enable them in ESP-IDF with CONFIG_ESP32S3_AI_VECTOR=y.

Advanced: Distributed Inference Across Multiple ESP32-S3 Boards

When a single ESP32-S3 cannot fit your model, you can distribute inference across multiple boards using ESP-NOW, Espressif’s connectionless wireless protocol.

Architecture

The wladimiravila project demonstrates a 56M-parameter model distributed across 3 ESP32-S3 boards:

  • Board 0 (Coordinator): Input tokenization, first embedding layers, output decoding
  • Board 1 (Worker): Middle transformer layers (layers 2–4)
  • Board 2 (Worker): Final transformer layers (layers 5–6), output projection

Each board holds a portion of the model weights in its 16 MB flash. Intermediate activations are transmitted via ESP-NOW, which has a typical latency of 2–5ms per packet.

Implementation Sketch

// Coordinator board
void coordinator_infer(int32_t* input_ids) {
    int32_t embeddings[256];
    embed_lookup(input_ids, 4, embeddings);
    
    // Send embeddings to Board 1 via ESP-NOW
    esp_now_send(board1_mac, (uint8_t*)embeddings, sizeof(embeddings));
    
    // Wait for final logits from Board 2
    int32_t logits[1000];
    esp_now_receive(board2_mac, (uint8_t*)logits, sizeof(logits));
    
    int token = argmax(logits, 1000);
    printf("Generated: %s\n", detokenize(token));
}

This approach scales to much larger models but introduces wireless latency. The distributed setup achieves approximately 5 seconds per token for the 56M-parameter model, which is usable for non-real-time applications like autonomous agents.

Troubleshooting Common Issues (PSRAM, Flash Size, Inference Speed)

PSRAM Not Detected

Symptom: esp_psram_init() returns ESP_FAIL or the system crashes when allocating PSRAM.

Solution: Ensure your board has PSRAM populated (N16R8 variant has 8 MB PSRAM, N16R2 has 2 MB). Verify the PSRAM configuration in menuconfig:

  • Enable SPIRAM and set to Octal SPI PSRAM
  • Set PSRAM clock to 80 MHz (not 120 MHz, which can cause instability)
  • Enable SPIRAM_USE_CAPS_ALLOC for dynamic allocation

Model Too Large for Flash

Symptom: Build fails with partition overflow, or the device crashes during model loading.

Solution:

  • Reduce model size with more aggressive quantization (4-bit instead of INT8)
  • Prune less important weights (structured pruning can remove 30–50% of parameters with minimal accuracy loss)
  • Use a larger flash module (N16R8 has 16 MB flash; custom boards can use up to 64 MB)

Slow Inference Speed

Symptom: Inference takes 5+ seconds per token.

Solution:

  • Enable AI vector instructions in ESP-IDF (CONFIG_ESP32S3_AI_VECTOR=y)
  • Optimize for sequential flash reads (restructure weight access patterns)
  • Reduce sequence length (shorter context = faster inference)
  • Use INT8 or 4-bit quantization (smaller weights = less flash bandwidth)
  • Consider distributed inference for models over 2M parameters

Random Crashes During Inference

Symptom: ESP32-S3 resets or throws a panic during model inference.

Solution:

  • Check stack size: increase CONFIG_ESP_MAIN_TASK_STACK_SIZE to 8192 or higher
  • Ensure all large buffers are allocated in PSRAM, not internal SRAM
  • Verify flash timing: reduce SPI flash frequency if using long PCB traces
  • Add cache prefetch hints for sequential weight access

FAQ

What is the smallest language model that can run on ESP32-S3?

The smallest practical SLM for ESP32-S3 has around 100K–312K parameters. The esp32-gpio-llm project runs a 312K-parameter model in 1.2 MB of FP32 weights, achieving 150ms–1.5s inference latency. Even smaller models (50K–100K parameters) are possible for highly constrained tasks like binary classification or keyword spotting.

Do I need external PSRAM to run an SLM on ESP32-S3?

Yes, for any model larger than about 50K parameters. The ESP32-S3 has only 512 KB of internal SRAM, and the operating system and runtime consume roughly 100 KB of that. External PSRAM (2–8 MB) is required for model weights and activation buffers. Use the N16R8 module variant which includes 8 MB PSRAM and 16 MB flash.

Can I train the model directly on the ESP32-S3?

No — the ESP32-S3 lacks the memory and compute to train even a small language model. Training is done on a PC or cloud GPU using PyTorch or TensorFlow, then the trained model is exported to ONNX, quantized, and compiled for the ESP32-S3. The microcontroller handles inference only.

How does distributed inference work across multiple ESP32-S3 boards?

Distributed inference splits the model layers across multiple ESP32-S3 boards connected via ESP-NOW (Espressif’s wireless protocol). Each board holds a portion of the model weights in its flash. Intermediate activations are transmitted wirelessly between boards. The wladimiravila project demonstrates a 56M-parameter model across 3 boards with ~5s per token latency.

What is the power consumption of an ESP32-S3 running SLM inference?

An ESP32-S3 running SLM inference consumes approximately 80–160 mA at 3.3V (264–528 mW) during active inference, and can drop to deep sleep mode at ~10 µA between inference events. This makes battery-powered SLM deployments feasible for applications that run inference intermittently, such as sensor nodes or voice-triggered assistants.
